highlights: The US-Soviet Joint Commission convened on 20 March at Duk Soo Palace to discuss establishing a unified provisional Korean democratic government.
Ordinance No. 60 dissolved all Japanese-era provincial and local government councils and impounded their official records and funds.
The New Korea Company Limited was established under Ordinance No. 52, taking over the former Japanese Oriental Development Company's extensive assets.
Military Government announced plans to sell formerly Japanese-owned agricultural lands to landless Korean tenant farmers on long-term credit.
USAMGIK enforced a strict rice collection program and prepared urban rationing in Seoul amidst severe food shortages and public criticism.
Korean civil police were granted authority to arrest US military personnel caught committing serious felonies, while third-degree interrogation methods were prohibited.
Repatriation of Koreans from Japan reached 831,387 cumulative returnees, while Japanese nationals remaining in South Korea dropped below 1,200.

summary: Covering March 1946, this monthly summation documents the administration of the United States Army Military Government in Korea (USAMGIK) during a crucial phase of post-liberation occupation. Major political developments include the opening of the first formal sessions of the United States–Soviet Joint Commission at Duk Soo Palace on 20 March to discuss Korean independence, the dissolution of Japanese-era local councils under Ordinance No. 60, the reorganization of the Oriental Development Company into the New Korea Company Limited (Ordinance No. 52), and massive, orderly rightist celebrations on Korean Independence Day (Sam Il Day). Economically, the occupation government struggled with critical shortages of food, fertilizer, and timber. It enforced a controversial rice seizure and urban rationing program in Seoul, banned opium poppy cultivation, received emergency shipments of industrial chemicals and coal from Japan, and restarted damaged textile and industrial mills. In social affairs, extensive smallpox and typhus vaccination programs were executed, educational planning was instituted alongside bans on student political activism, and relief supplies were distributed. For historians, this report offers vital empirical data on repatriation flows, vested Japanese property management, interzone relations, and the administrative mechanics of early American military rule in South Korea.
